title: A Different Kind of Loyalty
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 26 of 40
content:
Two days before the hearing, Snape received his formal notice to appear before the Wizengamot.

He read it in silence.

Then he corrected the date.

I looked over his shoulder.

“They wrote the twenty-third.”

“The hearing is the twenty-fourth.”

“You're being summoned by the government and your first response is proofreading.”

“The government should be more careful.”

“Terrifying priorities.”

He handed me the parchment.

His fingers were cold.

That was the only sign he was frightened.

The hearing would not be a criminal trial in the strict sense. Too much had already been established by testimony after the battle. Kingsley Shacklebolt had authorized a special review of Snape's wartime actions, teaching record, Death Eater involvement, and status under post-war amnesty provisions.

In other words, the Ministry had invented a room large enough to contain every contradiction and invited several dozen people to argue inside it.

Snape hated it.

“You do not have to attend,” he told me.

“I know.”

“You are not a witness unless called.”

“I know.”

“There will be press outside.”

“I know.”

“You should stay here.”

“No.”

His jaw tightened.

“You are not necessary.”

The word might once have hurt.

Now I heard the fear beneath it.

“I know that too.”

He looked at me.

“I am coming because I want to.”

His expression shifted.

“That is an insufficient reason.”

“For you?”

“For exposing yourself to spectacle.”

“I'm an adult.”

“A debatable condition.”

“Still coming.”

He turned away.

I let him.

Later that evening, I found him in the research lab staring at a row of potion bottles he had already labeled twice.

“You're nervous.”

“No.”

“You alphabetized.”

His head snapped toward the shelf.

I smiled.

“Domestic cupboard rules?”

“Leave.”

“No.”

He exhaled through his nose.

I took the stool beside him.

“What are you afraid they'll decide?”

His face closed.

I waited.

At last he said, “That nothing I did afterward matters.”

The answer surprised me.

I had expected imprisonment. Loss of wand rights. Public condemnation.

Not this.

“You think they'll reduce you to joining Voldemort.”

“Yes.”

“And the opposite?” I asked. “Are you afraid they'll decide what you did afterward erases everything before?”

Snape looked at me sharply.

“Yes.”

There it was.

The impossible position.

Condemnation felt false.

Absolution felt false.

He wanted a judgment complicated enough to hurt correctly.

“Maybe the hearing can't give you that,” I said.

His expression darkened.

“Then what is its purpose?”

“Legal status. Public record. Consequences.”

“Meaning?”

“Meaning maybe the Ministry is bad at souls.”

A pause.

Then, unexpectedly, Snape laughed.

“That may be the first intelligent thing you have said all month.”

“I'm putting it in the report.”

“Please do.”

We sat in silence.

I looked at his left forearm. The Mark was hidden under his sleeve.

“Lucius asked you not to testify against him.”

“Yes.”

“Are you going to?”

“Yes.”

“Even if it hurts his case badly?”

“Yes.”

“Were you loyal to him once?”

Snape's mouth tightened.

“I thought so.”

“What changed?”

“Everything.”

“That is vague.”

“You ask questions with answers too large for the room.”

“Try.”

He looked down at his hands.

“I once thought loyalty meant remaining,” he said. “Staying beside people. Protecting secrets. Refusing betrayal.”

I listened.

“It took me an embarrassing amount of time to understand that loyalty to a person can become disloyalty to every principle one claims to possess.”

“That sounds like Dumbledore.”

His eyes narrowed.

“It does not.”

“It does a little.”

“Retract it.”

“No.”

His mouth twitched.

“What does loyalty mean now?” I asked.

Snape was quiet.

“Telling the truth when silence would be kinder to myself.”

That landed heavily.

“That's what the hearing is?”

“Partly.”

“And Lucius?”

“Yes.”

“And me?”

The question escaped.

Snape went still.

I had not meant to place myself beside war and testimony.

Too late.

He turned toward me fully.

“What about you?”

“What does loyalty look like with me?”

His face changed in small ways.

Tension at the mouth.

Thought behind the eyes.

Fear, perhaps.

Then he held out his hand.

I placed mine in it.

“This,” he said.

I waited.

“When I am angry, I do not get to injure you and call it honesty.”

His thumb moved across my knuckles.

“When I am afraid, I do not get to decide for you what you should know.”

I breathed carefully.

“When you say no, I stop.”

My throat tightened.

“When you choose to leave a room, I do not make leaving a punishment.”

That one hurt in a way he probably did not know.

“And when you choose to stay?” I asked.

His grip tightened.

“I attempt to believe you.”

That was Severus Snape's version of romance.

Not forever.

Not destiny.

An attempt to believe a choice offered freely.

I lifted his hand and pressed my mouth to his knuckles.

He froze.

The contact was brief.

When I lowered his hand, his expression had gone completely unguarded.

“Was that all right?” I asked.

“Yes.”

His voice was rough.

“Do you want me to do it again?”

A pause.

“Yes.”

I did.

This time his eyes closed.

The moment felt more intimate than a kiss might have.

Perhaps because it was not stolen by momentum.

It was asked.

Answered.

Repeated.

Outside, snow tapped softly against the narrow windows.

The hearing waited two days away.

For that evening, loyalty meant nothing grander than staying beside him while he reorganized bottles that did not need reorganizing.

When I left, they were alphabetical.

I did not mention it.
